videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson09.sa

An ethanol molecule has fewer electrons than butane, yet ethanol boils about eighty degrees higher and mixes with water. See how the polar O–H bond lets alcohol molecules hydrogen bond, how to name alcohols by IUPAC rules and classify them as primary, secondary or tertiary, and why the carbon chain sets the boiling point and solubility trends along the series and across isomers. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson12.sa

Antibodies can't reach a virus once it's inside your cells. So how does your body find the infected ones? Follow a virus into an airway cell and see how cells display pieces of the proteins they make (antigen presentation), why a T cell receptor fits only a displayed piece, how dendritic cells select the right T cells in a lymph node, how helper T cells coordinate with cytokines, and how cytotoxic T cells make infected cells self-destruct (apoptosis). With the innate NK cells as a contrast, and an Australian discovery: Doherty and Zinkernagel, Canberra, 1973. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

videos.description:

The same ethanol molecule can start as ethene from crude oil or natural gas, as a haloalkane in a flask, or as sugar fermented by yeast. See why ethene hydration is written as an equilibrium and run at high pressure with recycling, why a haloalkane swaps its halogen for an OH group when heated under reflux with aqueous hydroxide, and why fermentation needs yeast, warmth and no air, shown with a school setup and the limewater test. Then judge each route by its feedstock, conditions, rate and how the ethanol is separated. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson11.sa

E10 petrol is up to ten percent ethanol, yet litre for litre ethanol carries less energy than petrol. Balance complete and incomplete combustion equations for alcohols, see why soot means too little oxygen, and see why each extra CH₂ adds about 650 kJ/mol to the enthalpy of combustion. Then compare fuels per gram, see why an alcohol's oxygen lowers its energy, and weigh ethanol against petrol: the same products, but carbon recently taken from the air against fossil carbon, with the energy, land and water ethanol needs and the costs of extracting hydrocarbons from the Earth. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.originalTitle: How Hygiene, Quarantine and Herd Immunity Stop Disease Spreading | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lessons, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson15.sa and https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson21.sa

In 1847, washing hands in a chlorine solution cut deaths in a Vienna maternity clinic, years before germ theory was accepted. Why? Find the link each control measure breaks in the chain of spread. See how soap and water remove microbes, why alcohol rub works less well on norovirus, and how environmental management keeps working on its own. Then follow measles, which hygiene can't stop: isolation and its catch, contact tracing, quarantine and the incubation period, and border biosecurity. Finally, see how herd immunity stops outbreaks and why measles needs about 95% vaccination coverage, then judge each measure by four criteria. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson11.sa

A spirit burner under a can of water catches only about half the energy of each alcohol, so how can you still compare methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol fairly? Set up the investigation with a draught shield and lid, weigh the burner with its cap on, and heat each alcohol for the same temperature rise. Calculate the molar enthalpy of combustion (water in q, fuel in n), see why the comparison is reliable even though each value is low, trace heat loss, incomplete combustion and evaporation to their effect on ΔH, match each improvement to its cause, and write the risk assessment for the four alcohols. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.title: Antibiotics vs Antivirals: How They Work and Why Resistance Spreads | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Antibiotics vs Antivirals: How They Work and Why Resistance Spreads | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson16.sa

Antibiotics do nothing for the flu, but a flu antiviral can shorten it if it's taken early. Why? See how selective toxicity works: penicillin stops bacteria building their walls, other antibiotics block bacterial ribosomes, and a virus has neither. Then see how antivirals block steps the virus needs, such as oseltamivir trapping new flu viruses on the cell, why the flu antiviral helps most when started early, and why most antivirals are narrow and few. Finally, see how drugs select resistance, how bacteria share resistance genes on plasmids, why HIV is treated with three drugs at once, and how to assess the effectiveness of each class. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

Practise three HSC-style spirit-burner calculations. Find the molar enthalpy of combustion of methanol from raw burner data and the percentage of its heat that reached the water. videos.title: Mosquito Control: Insecticides, Sterile Males and Wolbachia | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Mosquito Control: Insecticides, Sterile Males and Wolbachia | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson17.sa

In the 1950s, DDT spraying bred resistant mosquitoes. In 2014, Townsville released more mosquitoes, and local dengue stayed rare for about ten years. How? Follow the Aedes aegypti life cycle from eggs on a bucket wall to a biting female, and see how removing breeding water works as environmental management. Then see how pesticides work, why bed nets suit night-biting malaria mosquitoes but not day-biting Aedes, and how insecticides select resistance and harm other species. Finally, compare sterile males, genetically engineered males and Wolbachia, and judge each method on how much it cuts transmission, how long it lasts, its cost and what else it might harm. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

videos.originalTitle: Reactions of Alcohols: Dehydration, Substitution with HX and Oxidation | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson12.sa

Warm acidified dichromate with ethanol and it turns green; warm it with 2-methylpropan-2-ol and it stays orange. See how dehydration removes water to make an alkene (and why it is hydration run backwards), how a hydrogen halide swaps the OH for a halogen, and how oxidation depends on the alcohol's class: primary alcohols give an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid, secondary alcohols give a ketone, and tertiary alcohols usually do not react. Learn when to distil and when to reflux. Two exam-style questions at the end.

Propanal and propanone have the same formula, C₃H₆O, yet only one turns a test tube into a silver mirror. See where the carbonyl group sits in an aldehyde and a ketone, how to name both by IUPAC rules, why their boiling points sit between alkanes and alcohols, and why Tollens' reagent, Fehling's solution and acidified dichromate react with aldehydes but not ketones. Then use a test to identify the product of an alcohol oxidation. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.originalTitle: Validity, Reliability, Accuracy and Improvements: Practical Questions | HSC Exam Skills
videos.description:
Full lessons, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12
https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12

Practical questions ask whether a method is valid, reliable or accurate, then ask you to improve it, and NESA's marking feedback keeps asking for a clearer understanding of the three words. Learn what each word asks (right target, repeats agree, close to true), a three-step move for every answer (word, feature, fix), and why "repeat it" fixes reliability but not an error that pushes every trial the same way. See a worked spirit-burner question, then try two training questions, one in Chemistry (reliability against accuracy) and one in Biology (a validity flaw in an agar-plate test). All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.
